title: The AI-native law firm: regulatory innovation and the fundamental restructuring of legal service delivery
pub: International Bar Association (IBA) — author at Khaitan & Co, Mumbai
author: Saranya Mishra

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Mishra accepts that AI requires structural redesign and pressures hourly billing and staffing leverage, but shifts the principal mechanism away from buyer-side organisational absorption. She instead centres regulatory permission, capital-backed AI-native providers and technology-first economics, predicting displacement of traditional partnerships more strongly than the cluster’s contested, buyer-led account supports.
qs: A new category of legal service provider has emerged – ‘the AI-native law firm’ – characterised not by the retrofitting of technology onto traditional structures, but by the integration of AI as the fundamental lever of service delivery from inception.

Traditional firms face a fundamental choice: evolve business models to reflect that AI, not human labour pyramids, constitutes the primary leverage mechanism, or accept gradual displacement by competitors operating with structurally superior economics.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Mishra shares the cluster’s view that AI is structurally reconfiguring legal-service delivery and that safeguards remain necessary, but redirects the emphasis from bounded, supervised workflow gains and competence risks toward AI-native firms, autonomous delivery, alternative pricing and business-model displacement. Her stronger claims that transformation is inevitable and AI will replace human labour pyramids as the primary source of leverage go beyond the cluster’s cautious, evidence-limited conclusions.

st.t: Workflow control: Foundation models challenge specialist interfaces
st.an: The source shifts the focus from competition for lawyers’ software interface to the restructuring of legal-service delivery itself. It argues that AI capabilities and permissive ownership regimes enable AI-native firms to sell substantive legal work, while recognising safeguards and public-risk monitoring.
qs: These regulatory frameworks represent a philosophical shift: accepting that legal service delivery can be fundamentally reimagined when appropriate safeguards and accountability mechanisms exist.

Unlike incremental efficiency tools that marginally improve existing workflows, current AI systems can perform substantive legal work at speeds and costs that fundamentally challenge traditional economic assumptions.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: Mishra accepts the cluster’s operating-model thesis and materially extends it by identifying regulatory authorisation, AI-native delivery architecture, alternative pricing and buyer diversification as mechanisms shifting work toward new providers. Her conclusions are more categorical than the cluster’s cautious synthesis, treating transformation and displacement as increasingly inevitable despite relying partly on forecasts and firm examples.
qs: A new category of legal service provider has emerged – ‘the AI-native law firm’ – characterised not by the retrofitting of technology onto traditional structures, but by the integration of AI as the fundamental lever of service delivery from inception.

Thomson Reuters’ 2025 ALSP Report reveals that 85 per cent of corporate legal departments use traditional law firms, but 44 per cent now purchase directly from independent Alternative Legal Service Providers, with 33 per cent using law firm affiliate ALSPs.[[11]](#_edn11) This diversification reflects client willingness to experiment with non-traditional providers when value propositions are compelling.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI will restructure legal-service production, staffing leverage, pricing and provider competition rather than simply eliminate lawyers. It materially extends that account by identifying regulatory liberalisation and outside capital as additional enablers of AI-native delivery. Its claims of autonomous capability and inevitable transformation are substantially more bullish than the cluster’s emphasis on bounded automation and uncertain market-wide effects.
qs: ## Conclusion  The emergence of AI-native law firms represents a genuine structural shift, not incremental evolution.

Regulatory willingness to authorise novel models, technological capabilities enabling autonomous legal work, economic pressure for alternative pricing and capital availability converge to make this transformation inevitable rather than speculative.

Its software-like scalability claims are explicitly an investment thesis rather than established evidence, making it more bullish but not opposed to the cluster’s caution.

st.t: AI investment: Delivery businesses may capture more value
st.an: The source strongly supports the proposition that integrated AI-native legal-service providers may capture more value than software-only vendors. It argues that technology-driven delivery can replace associate leverage, align pricing with efficiency and achieve superior scalability, while offering firm examples as illustrations. Its claims of inevitability, software-like margins and displacement are materially stronger than the synthesis and remain largely predictive rather than demonstrated.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI-enabled delivery can restructure legal-service business models without requiring wholesale lawyer replacement. It points to existing regulated AI-native firms as competitive alternatives to traditional practices, but its claims of comparable quality at a fraction of the cost and generational market restructuring are forecasts not substantiated by comparative performance data.
qs: The question confronting the profession is not whether AI-native firms will exist – they already do, with regulatory approval and substantial capital backing – but rather what role traditional firms will play in a market where technology-first competitors can deliver comparable quality at a fraction of the cost.
The answer will probably determine the structure of legal practice for the next generation.

kp.k: AI-native firms organise delivery around technology from inception
kp.d: Mishra argues that AI-native firms represent structural transformation rather than incremental technology adoption. The article identifies regulatory innovation, technological capability, client economic pressure and capital availability as converging enablers, and concludes that transformation is inevitable; this is the author's interpretation and prediction.
qs: A new category of legal service provider has emerged – ‘the AI-native law firm’ – characterised not by the retrofitting of technology onto traditional structures, but by the integration of AI as the fundamental lever of service delivery from inception.

Regulatory willingness to authorise novel models, technological capabilities enabling autonomous legal work, economic pressure for alternative pricing and capital availability converge to make this transformation inevitable rather than speculative.

kp.k: Garfield authorisation combines AI delivery with regulatory safeguards
kp.d: The article reports that the SRA authorised Garfield.Law Ltd in May 2025 as the first firm delivering legal services entirely through AI. Its small claims debt recovery assistant covers claims up to £10,000, from calculating debt to filing for default judgment, with per-document pricing. Authorisation requires confidentiality, conflict controls, user approval at each stage and restrictions on proposing case law. The reported model therefore includes user approvals despite the article's entirely-through-AI description; SRA chief executive Paul Phillip also acknowledges public risks requiring monitoring.
qs: In May 2025, the UK Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA) made legal history by approving Garfield.Law Ltd as the first law firm authorised to deliver legal services entirely through AI technology.
The firm charges on a per-document basis rather than hourly rates, fundamentally departing from traditional economic models.

The SRA’s authorisation came with strict safeguards including client confidentiality protection, conflict avoidance mechanisms, user approval at each stage and controls preventing AI from proposing case law – addressing concerns about AI hallucinations.

kp.k: Arizona permits nonlawyer ownership of AI-augmented legal providers
kp.d: The article reports that Arizona's ABS programme enabled Eudia Counsel to operate with non-lawyer ownership, providing corporate contracting, M&A due diligence and other complex services. It places Eudia alongside affiliated firms launched by KPMG, Axiom, LegalZoom and Elevate, interpreting these regulatory frameworks as acceptance of redesigned delivery where safeguards and accountability exist.
qs: Similarly, Arizona’s Alternative Business Structure (ABS) programme has enabled Eudia Counsel to operate as an ‘AI-augmented law firm’ with non-lawyer ownership, to support corporate clients with contracting, M&A due diligence and other complex legal needs.
It joins KPMG, Axiom, LegalZoom, and Elevate, all of which have launched affiliated firms under the ABS programme.

kp.k: NormAI combines legal engineering with institutional service delivery
kp.d: The article reports November 2025 Blackstone funding to launch Norm Law, described as an AI-native full-service firm for global institutional clients. NormAI's methodology combines a no-code platform with over 35 lawyers trained to convert workflows into large language model-driven agents. Mishra treats clients collectively managing over $30tn in assets as evidence that these models can address sophisticated institutional needs rather than only routine consumer work.
qs: NormAI’s proprietary ‘Legal Engineering’ methodology combines their no-code AI platform with over 35 lawyers trained to convert legal workflows into large language model-driven AI agents.
The firm serves clients collectively managing over $30tn in assets, demonstrating that AI-native models can address sophisticated institutional requirements, not merely routine consumer matters.

kp.k: Crosby illustrates faster review and accumulating client knowledge
kp.d: The article reports Crosby's $5.8m funding from Sequoia Capital and Bain Capital Ventures and a median contract-review turnaround of 58 minutes. It attributes the proposition that customer-specific knowledge bases become more sophisticated over time to Sequoia's investment thesis, using this to argue that AI can accumulate institutional memory.
qs: Similarly, Crosby – which raised $5.8m from Sequoia Capital and Bain Capital Ventures – provides AI-powered contract review with a median turnaround of 58 minutes.

Sequoia’s investment thesis emphasises Crosby’s ability to build customer-specific knowledge bases that become more sophisticated over time, highlighting how AI systems can develop institutional memory that compounds value rather than remaining static.

kp.k: Lawhive examination performance supports claims of substantive capability
kp.d: Mishra reports that Lawhive's Lawrence scored 81 per cent on the Solicitors Qualifying Examination against a 55 per cent pass threshold. The author interprets this examination result as demonstrating paralegal- or junior-lawyer-level proficiency and substantive legal analysis rather than clerical automation.
qs: Lawhive’s AI assistant ‘Lawrence’ scored 81 per cent on the Solicitors Qualifying Examination, well above the 55 per cent pass threshold, demonstrating proficiency at paralegal or junior lawyer level.
This is not automation of clerical tasks – it represents AI performing substantive legal analysis.

kp.k: Covenant substitutes technology for associate-based economic leverage
kp.d: Against the traditional margin between associate salaries and billing rates, the article presents Covenant's technology-led model: $4m seed funding, six lawyers and limited partnership agreement reviews at $900 per document, approximately 90 per cent below traditional pricing. It reports 80-90 per cent reductions in time and cost as an example of altered service economics.
qs: The traditional law firm model relies on leverage: partners supervising associates who perform the bulk of billable work, creating economic returns through the margin between associate salaries and billing rates.

The firm operates with only six lawyers handling highly leveraged work, offering limited partnership agreement reviews at $900 per document – approximately 90 per cent less than traditional pricing – while achieving 80-90 per cent reductions in time and cost.

kp.k: Technology leverage could reduce staffing requirements substantially
kp.d: Mishra proposes that a technology-leveraged firm with under ten lawyers could match a traditional 60-lawyer firm's output. This is framed as potential rather than a measured comparison. The author further asserts that logarithmically scaling technology costs and fixed investments replace linearly scaling labour and variable human capital costs.
qs: A technology-leveraged firm with under ten lawyers can potentially match the output of a traditional firm requiring 60 lawyers under the pyramid model.
The cost structure transforms: technology costs scale logarithmically while human labour scales linearly. Fixed technology investments replace variable human capital costs.

kp.k: Partner-only hybrid firms redirect junior work to AI
kp.d: The article presents Pierson Ferdinand, launched with over 130 partners and zero junior lawyers, as a hybrid staffing model. Senior partners use software including Harvey AI for first drafts and routine tasks previously performed by associates.
qs: Pierson Ferdinand, launched with over 130 partners but zero junior lawyers, exemplifies a hybrid approach.
Senior partners use platforms such as Harvey AI for first drafts and routine work traditionally performed by associates.

kp.k: Client cost pressure favours alternative pricing and providers
kp.d: Mishra argues that corporate departments' need to reduce external spending while maintaining quality favours fixed fees, per-transaction charges and subscriptions over hourly billing. Citing Thomson Reuters' 2025 ALSP Report, the article reports 85 per cent of corporate legal departments using traditional firms, 44 per cent purchasing directly from independent ALSPs and 33 per cent using law firm affiliate ALSPs. The author interprets this diversification as willingness to try non-traditional providers with compelling value propositions.
qs: Traditional hourly billing creates misaligned incentives: the slower the work, the higher the revenue.
AI-native firms offering fixed fees, per-transaction pricing or subscription models address this fundamental tension.

Thomson Reuters’ 2025 ALSP Report reveals that 85 per cent of corporate legal departments use traditional law firms, but 44 per cent now purchase directly from independent Alternative Legal Service Providers, with 33 per cent using law firm affiliate ALSPs.

kp.k: Unmet civil legal needs offer market expansion opportunities
kp.d: Citing the Legal Services Corporation, the article states that more than 50 million low-income Americans receive inadequate help for 92 per cent of civil legal problems. It also identifies UK small businesses' unpaid invoices as claims uneconomic to pursue under traditional fees. Mishra argues that providers such as Garfield target previously unprofitable markets, expanding access and the overall legal services market.
qs: More than 50 million low-income Americans receive inadequate legal help for 92 per cent of civil legal problems.
In the UK, small businesses are owed billions in unpaid invoices but cannot economically pursue claims under traditional fee structures.
AI-native firms like Garfield explicitly target markets traditional firms cannot profitably serve, expanding the overall market for legal services.

kp.k: External capital supports scale and regulated-provider acquisitions
kp.d: The article reports NormAI's total funding exceeding $140m and presents capital availability as an enabling factor. It describes an investment thesis of software-like margins, human-quality outcomes and low marginal costs, rather than reporting measured industry-wide economics. Lawhive's September 2025 acquisition of Woodstock Legal Services, described with the qualification that it was believed to be the first such acquisition by an AI company, is interpreted as confidence in combining technology platforms and regulated legal entities.
qs: NormAI’s total funding exceeds $140m from investors including Blackstone, Bain Capital, Vanguard, Citi, and Marc Benioff,
Technology-enabled firms can operate at software-like margins while delivering human-quality outcomes.

Notably, Google-backed Lawhive’s acquisition of traditional UK firm Woodstock Legal Services in September 2025 – believed to be the first acquisition of a traditional law firm by an AI company – signals capital’s confidence in vertical integration strategies combining technology platforms with regulated legal entities.

kp.k: Hourly billing faces predicted structural revenue compression
kp.d: Mishra conditionally argues that AI performing trained legal work in minutes at near-zero marginal cost undermines the scarcity underlying partnership economics. The author recommends business-model change rather than merely improving efficiency while retaining hourly billing, and predicts gradual displacement for firms that fail to adapt. Reported LexisNexis research finds 47 per cent of lawyers and 55 per cent of general counsel believe AI will change billing; these are expectations, not observed billing changes.
qs: If AI can perform work previously requiring three years of legal training in minutes, at marginal cost approaching zero, the traditional leverage model faces structural revenue compression.
LexisNexis research shows 47 per cent of lawyers believe AI will change how firms bill for services, with 55 per cent of general counsel holding this view.

Traditional firms face a fundamental choice: evolve business models to reflect that AI, not human labour pyramids, constitutes the primary leverage mechanism, or accept gradual displacement by competitors operating with structurally superior economics.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Mishra claims that regulatory innovation enables firms built around AI delivery rather than traditional lawyer staffing.
pts.d: The author presents the SRA's May 2025 authorisation of Garfield and Arizona's ABS framework as concrete enablers of new service models. Garfield provides small-claims debt recovery up to £10,000, with per-document pricing and user approval at each stage. Eudia Counsel is described separately as AI-augmented, serving corporate contracting, M&A due diligence and other complex needs under a nonlawyer-ownership regime. Mishra's broader interpretation is that regulators are accepting fundamentally redesigned delivery when safeguards and accountability exist; the examples do not all represent the same degree of autonomy.

pts.k: Mishra claims that AI now performs substantive legal work, including institutional work, rather than merely automating clerical tasks.
pts.d: The author uses Norm Law's institutional-client positioning and NormAI's legal-engineering workforce to argue that AI-native delivery extends beyond routine consumer work. She reports Crosby's median contract-review turnaround of 58 minutes and describes customer-specific knowledge bases as accumulating institutional memory. She interprets Lawhive's reported 81 per cent SQE score, against a stated 55 per cent pass threshold, as demonstrating paralegal- or junior-lawyer-level proficiency.

pts.k: Mishra claims that technology replaces associate-to-partner staffing leverage, permitting much smaller teams and lower prices.
pts.d: The author describes Covenant's six-lawyer team, $900 limited partnership agreement reviews, prices approximately 90 per cent below traditional pricing, and reported 80–90 per cent time and cost reductions. She then advances a potential output comparison: fewer than ten lawyers in a technology-leveraged firm could match a traditional 60-lawyer firm. She asserts that technology costs scale logarithmically rather than linearly and that fixed technology investments replace variable human-capital costs. Pierson Ferdinand's reported launch with over 130 partners and no juniors is offered as a hybrid example, with senior lawyers using Harvey AI for first drafts and routine associate work.

pts.k: Mishra predicts structural pressure on hourly billing as AI shortens work and clients seek lower-cost alternatives.
pts.d: The author argues that corporate legal departments' cost and quality requirements favour fixed-fee, per-transaction and subscription offerings. She interprets purchases from ALSPs as evidence of openness to nontraditional providers. She predicts that firms cannot simply adopt AI while retaining unchanged hourly economics because clients will not pay equivalent amounts for work completed much faster. The LexisNexis percentages presented are respondents' expectations about billing change, not measured changes in billing practices.

pts.k: Mishra claims that AI-native firms can expand the legal-services market by serving unmet civil legal needs and uneconomic small claims.
pts.d: The author connects low-income Americans' unmet civil legal needs and UK small businesses' unpaid invoices to demand for lower-cost delivery. Garfield is the concrete example of a provider targeting claims that traditional fee structures make uneconomic. This is an access-to-justice and market-expansion claim, distinct from enterprise legal-spend savings.

pts.k: Mishra claims that outside capital enables scalable AI-native firms and technology-company integration with regulated legal practices.
pts.d: The author cites NormAI funding exceeding $140 million, Crosby's $5.8 million and Covenant's $4 million as support for AI-native service models. She characterises the investment thesis as software-like margins, human-quality outcomes and low marginal costs for additional clients. She interprets Lawhive's September 2025 acquisition of Woodstock Legal Services as evidence of confidence in vertical integration, retaining the source's qualification that it is believed to be the first such acquisition.

pts.k: Mishra predicts an inevitable structural transformation in which traditional firms must redesign their business models or face gradual displacement.
pts.d: The author's central forecast is that regulatory permission, technical capability, alternative-pricing demand and investment together undermine the partnership model's assumption of scarce human legal intellect. She frames revenue compression conditionally on AI delivering trained-lawyer work in minutes at near-zero marginal cost, but states the overall transformation more categorically. Traditional firms' response is predicted to shape legal practice for the next generation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source supports its argument with regulatory announcements, company and investment reports, selected operating metrics, an examination result and legal-market surveys.
pts.d: Regulation: SRA announcements and Garfield's website support the authorisation, service scope and safeguards; an Eudia-hosted report supports the Arizona example. Capability and economics: NormAI announcements supply launch, funding and institutional-client claims; Artificial Lawyer reports supply Crosby, Covenant and Pierson Ferdinand examples; the Law Society Gazette is cited for Lawhive's examination result and acquisition. The reported SQE score is examination-based evidence, while turnaround, prices and savings are operating claims; none should be conflated with a general legal-work quality evaluation. Demand: the Thomson Reuters 2025 ALSP Report supplies the 85 per cent traditional-firm, 44 per cent independent-ALSP and 33 per cent affiliate-ALSP usage figures, which concern provider purchasing rather than AI adoption specifically. The Legal Services Corporation supplies justice-gap figures. LexisNexis research is invoked for billing expectations, without a corresponding bibliographic reference in the supplied text. The small-team output equivalence, logarithmic cost scaling, software-like margins and long-run displacement are authorial generalisations or predictions rather than separately documented comparative findings in the article.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Mishra describes an emerging transformation observable in 2025 and projects its consequences over the next generation, without a dated displacement forecast.
pts.d: Specific milestones include Garfield's May 2025 authorisation, Lawhive's September 2025 acquisition and Norm Law's November 2025 launch; references were accessed on 23 December 2025. The source distinguishes existing providers from prospective sector-wide effects through terms such as 'potentially' for output equivalence, 'gradual' for displacement and 'probably' for the next-generation outlook. Regulatory acceptance is conditioned on safeguards and accountability. Garfield's scope is debt recovery up to £10,000, with confidentiality protections, conflict controls, user approval at every stage and a prohibition on proposing case law. The low-marginal-cost scaling thesis applies once systems have been developed; revenue compression is framed around AI's ability to deliver formerly trained-lawyer work rapidly and cheaply. Despite references to entirely AI-based or autonomous delivery, the article also describes human legal engineers, senior-lawyer use of AI and explicitly augmented firms.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects span traditional partnerships, junior lawyers, AI-native providers, corporate buyers, institutional clients, underserved individuals and small businesses.
pts.d: Traditional partners and firms face pressure on associate-based leverage, hourly revenue and competitive positioning. Associates' first-draft and routine work shifts to AI in the hybrid example, while senior lawyers use the tools and lawyers trained in legal engineering convert workflows into agents; the article does not provide a quantified employment-loss forecast. AI-native firms and ABS-affiliated providers gain routes to outside investment and new delivery structures. Corporate legal departments and general counsel obtain alternative pricing and provider choices; institutional clients receive AI-supported contracting, diligence and broader legal services. Small businesses may pursue debts previously uneconomic to recover, and low-income individuals' unmet civil legal needs are presented as an additional demand source. Regulators and the public face ongoing confidentiality, conflict, hallucination and accountability concerns. Investors and technology companies participate through funding and acquisitions.
